sections.html:
MachineMacintosh SE, 512×342 black and white
SystemSystem 7.5.3
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly
Version2.0, the Macintosh release
SpeechMacinTalk, Apple's 1984 speech synthesiser
SavesInside the emulated Mac, in your browser.

The disk this came from carried MacinTalk beside the application — Apple's speech synthesiser, released in 1984 and quietly one of the reasons the Macintosh felt like the future. Reader Rabbit uses it to say the words aloud, and it has been installed into the System Folder here so that it does.

It does not sound good. It sounded extraordinary at the time.

Sorter puts words on a conveyor and asks the child to sort them by a shared letter, which is the quiet foundation the other three stand on.

Labeller shows an object and a set of words, and the child picks the one that names it.

Word Train is the one everybody remembers: carriages rolling past carrying three-letter words, each of which has to differ from the last by exactly one letter. cat, cot, cog, dog. It is a word ladder, and it is a genuinely elegant piece of teaching disguised as a train.

Matchup is a memory game played with words and pictures.

All four use the same pool of two hundred or so three-letter words, so a child who has played one is not starting cold in the next.

The Learning Company was founded in 1980 by Ann McCormick, Leslie Grimm, Teri Perl and Warren Robinett — Robinett being the Atari programmer who had hidden his own name inside Adventure and invented the video game easter egg in the process.

Their argument was that educational software should be built by people who understood how children actually learn, not by programmers adding a quiz to a game. Grimm, who wrote Reader Rabbit, had a doctorate and had taught reading.

It shows. The four games are not four themes on one drill; they attack the same skill from four directions, and the one everyone remembers — the train — is the one that teaches the most. Reader Rabbit sold for twenty years and became the name an entire category was measured against.

faq.q: Is this the original Reader Rabbit?
faq.a: It is the Macintosh release of the original, version 2.0, in black and white with all four games. Not the later CD-ROM Reader Rabbit titles, which are much bigger and quite different.
Yes, through MacinTalk, Apple's 1984 speech synthesiser, which shipped on the same disk and is installed here. It sounds like 1984, because it is.
Roughly four to seven — children who know their letters and are starting to put them together into words.

faq.q: Which game should we start with?
faq.a: Word Train. It is the most fun, and the one-letter-at-a-time word ladder is the idea the whole program is built around.

faq.q: Why is it black and white?
faq.a: The Macintosh it was written for was. The artwork is drawn in one-bit patterns and is surprisingly expressive for it.

Someone has stolen something from a European capital, and you have a week to catch them. You fly between cities, interview witnesses who tell you the thief was asking about the local currency, and work out which country that points at.

It is a detective game where the clues are geography, and it is the reason a generation of children could find Liechtenstein on a map.

This one shipped on two floppies: the game on the first and a 653K file of graphics on the second. Both are here, which is worth saying because a copy missing the second disk starts up and then tells you the graphics cannot be found — a common state for this title in the wild.

Everything is mouse-driven. You get a case, a destination and a deadline, and you spend the week flying, asking questions and narrowing down.

Each city gives you three places to ask questions. The answers are geographical: the suspect changed money into drachmas, or asked about a fjord, or mentioned a country with a red and white flag. Each one is a clue to the next country, not the current one.

Witnesses also describe the thief — hair colour, hobby, vehicle, and so on. Those go into the Police Dossiers, and once you have narrowed the suspect list to one person you issue a warrant. Catch the right thief without a warrant and they walk.

The clock is the real opponent. Travel costs hours, interviews cost hours, and a wrong flight can cost you the case. Later ranks give you less time and vaguer clues.

sections.h: The game that taught by not teaching
sections.html:
Broderbund shipped the World edition in 1985 with a copy of The World Almanac in the box, and that was the whole design: the game would not tell you which country used the drachma, but the book on your desk would. It made the reference material the interface.

The Europe edition, from 1989, is the one that most rewards the trick. Thirty-odd countries in a small space, currencies and flags and languages that shade into each other, and clues that are only ever one step ahead of you. It is a geography lesson that never once announces itself as a geography lesson.

The series ran to more than a dozen titles, a long-running game show on PBS, and a cartoon. It is one of the few cases where educational software became genuinely mainstream culture.

faq.q: Do I need the almanac that came in the box?

You have to identify the thief as well as find them. Collect descriptions from witnesses, narrow the dossier to one suspect, and issue the warrant before you make the arrest, or they go free.

faq.q: Why do I keep running out of time?
faq.a: Travel and interviews both cost hours. Do not fly on a hunch: ask in all three places in a city first, and only move when the clues agree.

You do not choose your pieces. A queue down the side of the screen shows what is coming, and you must place the next one somewhere before you can see past it. That single rule is what turns a simple idea into a real game: you are always building with the wrong piece and planning around the two you can see.

The flow starts after a short delay and never stops. Reach the required length of pipe before it runs out and you go on to the next level, where it starts sooner and moves faster.

sections.h: How to be good at it
sections.html:
Build long, not direct. The target is a length of pipe, not a destination. A tight spiral in a corner scores the same as a sprawl and takes far less space.

Waste pieces deliberately. A piece you cannot use goes somewhere out of the way, not into your path. Placing a bad piece badly is the most common way to lose.

Use the crossover pieces. The one that carries flow in both directions is worth planning around — it lets your pipe cross its own run and is the basis of every long score.

Replacing costs time. You can drop a new piece on an existing one, and the flow keeps moving while you do. It is an emergency measure, not a strategy.

sections.h: Where it came from, and where it went
sections.html:
The Assembly Line, a small British studio, wrote it for the Amiga in 1989 as Pipe Mania. LucasArts published it in the United States as Pipe Dream, which is the name most people know and the name on this build.

It then spread further than almost any puzzle game of its generation, largely by being copied. The pipe-laying minigame that turns up in BioShock, in half the hacking sequences in games since, and in an enormous number of mobile titles is this, more or less unchanged. It became a piece of shared vocabulary rather than a game people remembered buying.

The original is a tighter thing than any of its descendants: no story around it, no reward screen, just a grid, a queue, and water that is already moving.

faq.a: Same game. The Assembly Line released it as Pipe Mania in Europe; LucasArts published it in the United States as Pipe Dream, and this is that build.

faq.q: Can I choose which piece to place?
faq.a: No, and that is the game. You get the next piece in the queue and can see a few ahead, so the skill is in building something that will accept whatever arrives.

faq.q: How do I get a long score?
faq.a: Spiral. The goal is total pipe length, not reaching a particular spot, so a dense coil in one corner beats a neat run across the board.
Practice with the flow switched off, so you can learn the pieces without the clock. It is on the title screen.

This is Super Munchers, the 1991 entry in MECC's Munchers series, which widened the idea from arithmetic and spelling to trivia — geography, history, science, sport and the rest.

The first thing it does is ask you to personalise the program with a name, which is how MECC software of this era identified a school's copy. Type anything and click OK.

After that it is one screen: a category on the banner, a grid of possible answers, a Muncher you steer, and Troggles that wander in and eat you if they reach you. Clear the correct answers on the board and you move up.

sections.h: What makes it harder than it looks
sections.html:
The categories are broad — European capitals, mammals, things that are liquid, US presidents — and the wrong answers are chosen to be plausible rather than silly. A board asking for mammals will have a shark on it somewhere.

The Troggles are the pressure. They come in several kinds and they do not all behave the same: some patrol in straight lines, some head for you, and one of them changes the squares as it passes, so an answer that was safe when you looked at it is not safe when you get there.

The result is a game where you cannot stand still and think. You have to know the answer before you are standing on it, which is a much better test than a quiz and the reason the series worked.

Number Munchers came first, in 1986, and it is the one most people name — multiples and factors and primes, eaten off a grid. Word Munchers did the same for spelling patterns. Super Munchers, in 1991, opened it up to general knowledge and added the two-player mode.

All of them come from MECC, the Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium, which also made The Oregon Trail and supplied a large share of the software in American school computer labs for two decades. The Munchers games were the other half of that shelf: the ones you were allowed to play when you had finished your work.

A note on availability: Number Munchers itself is genuinely hard to find for the Macintosh. The Apple II and MS-DOS versions are well preserved; the one Macintosh-specific upload is a truncated disk image with its catalogue missing, and the SoftKey CD-ROM keeps the game on its PC partition and gives the Mac side nothing but a bundled AOL installer. Super Munchers is the Munchers game that survives intact on the Mac, and it is the same idea with a wider net.

faq.a: No — it is Super Munchers, the 1991 trivia-based entry in the same series. The gameplay is identical; the categories are general knowledge instead of arithmetic.

Because a working Macintosh copy does not appear to survive. The only Mac-specific upload is a truncated image missing its catalogue, and the SoftKey hybrid CD keeps the game on the PC side. The Apple II and DOS versions are preserved and playable elsewhere.

faq.a: MECC software of this era asked each site to personalise its copy. Type anything and click OK.

intro:
In 1986 the Macintosh was an office machine with a small grey screen, and then Dark Castle arrived: a full-screen black-and-white castle drawn like a woodcut, bats that dive at your head, and rats, and a hunchback throwing rocks down a staircase at you.

It looked like nothing else on any computer, and it sounded like nothing else either. It is still the game people name when they argue the Macintosh was a real games machine.

It is hard, and it was meant to be. The controls split between the keyboard and the mouse — you run and jump with your left hand and aim with your right — and that division takes a while to stop feeling wrong. Turn the difficulty down in the Options menu for the first few attempts; the game does not think less of you.

The castle is three doors from the great hall, each leading to a short branch of rooms, and a fourth that opens onto the Black Knight at the end.

Mark Stephen Pierce drew it, and he drew it as though the one-bit screen were an engraving rather than a limitation. Everything is cross-hatched, stippled and heavy-lined, and the result has more depth than most colour games of the same year.

The sound is the other half. Dark Castle used digitised audio at a time when nearly every game used beeps — the bats screech, the rocks knock, and your character makes a genuinely upsetting noise when he falls. Silicon Beach recorded that material and shipped it, which is why the game took two floppies when most took one.

The programmer was Jonathan Gay, who was still in his teens. He went on to write the animation tool that became Macromedia Flash, so a reasonable share of the web's first decade traces back to the person who made these bats fly.

Throw while moving. Standing still to aim is how you get hit. The mouse aims independently of which way you are running, which is the whole point of the control scheme.

Crouch under things. S drops you low, and a great deal of what is thrown at you passes over a crouching character.

Rocks are limited. You carry a finite number and you will run out. Picking up more is often the real objective of a room.

The Trouble door first. Of the three branches it is the gentlest, and it teaches the movement without the rooms that punish it.

faq.q: Is this the original Dark Castle?
faq.a: Yes — version 1.2 of the 1986 Macintosh release, in black and white, as it shipped. Not Return to Dark Castle and not any of the later console conversions, which look and play quite differently.

faq.q: Why are the controls split between mouse and keyboard?
faq.a: Because you aim and move independently. The left hand runs, jumps and crouches; the right hand aims and throws. It is awkward for an hour and then it is the reason the game works.
Turn the difficulty down in the Options menu, and start with the Trouble door. The game was designed for people who would play it for weeks.
Yes, and in 1986 that was remarkable. It is most of why the game shipped on two disks and most of why people remember it.
Silicon Beach Software. Mark Stephen Pierce did the art, Jonathan Gay wrote the code — Gay later created the tool that became Macromedia Flash.

intro:
Gather the crystals, then fly to the exit. Do it while an increasing number of things that want to kill you fill the screen and learn your habits. There is no more to it than that, and Crystal Quest was one of the most-played Macintosh games ever released.

It is controlled entirely with the mouse, which sounds like a compromise and is in fact the reason it feels so good.

sections.html:

SystemSystem 7.5.3
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly
Version2.2.5
SavesHigh scores live inside the emulated Mac, in your browser.

Each wave drops a field of crystals and a set of enemies. Collect every crystal and the gate at the edge of the screen opens; fly through it and the next wave starts, harder.

The mouse control is absolute rather than relative — the ship is where the pointer is — so you can cross the screen instantly if your hand can move that fast. That is the skill ceiling, and it is high.

Enemies arrive by type and each behaves differently, which is the whole strategic layer. Some drift. Some home in. Some sit still and shoot. Some split when you kill them, and killing them at the wrong moment is worse than leaving them alone.

Mines are the ones that get you. They do not chase — they simply sit in the path between you and the last crystal, and the game is very good at placing them where you were about to go.

Finish a wave fast enough and you get a time bonus; dawdle and the game tells you, with some satisfaction, that there is no time bonus. Bonus crystals turn up too, and the rules are blunt about them: catch them to get a bonus, shoot them to lose it. Playing for score and playing to survive are genuinely different games.

Crystal Quest talks. It congratulates you, it insults you when you die, and the sampled voices are the thing every person who played it remembers first.

Patrick Buckland wrote the game; Casady & Greene, a Mac-only publisher with an unusually good ear for what the platform's users wanted, published it. Buckland went on to co-found Stainless Software, the studio behind Carmageddon. Casady & Greene closed in 2003, a Macintosh software house that outlived nearly all the others and is now mostly remembered for this and for Conflict Catcher.

The sound files are still on the disk with their copyright notices in the filenames, which is a small and rather charming piece of 1994 housekeeping.

sections.h: What the manual inside the game says
sections.html:
Crystal Quest carries its own instructions, and they are written in the same voice as the rest of it. The useful parts:

  • Extra lives come every 15,000 points up to wave 11, every 40,000 up to wave 26, and every 75,000 after that. Past wave 26 each one is expensive, so play for survival there.
  • Firing works with the mouse button or any letter key, and the shot always goes in the direction you are moving. To hit something, move towards it.
  • The space bar sets off a smart bomb, if you have one. It kills everything on the screen. The manual compares it to using an anti-aircraft gun on a mosquito. Collect the spare smart bombs that turn up in later waves.
  • Tab pauses. Command-S saves the game in progress. The number keys set the volume, from 0 (silent) to 9, and the manual says 8 sounds better than 9.
  • Delete switches between one and two players before a game starts, for passing the mouse to a friend.
  • Holding Option when you click to start puts a Mac II into super-fast mode. Scores set that way show in italics in the high-score table, so everyone can see how you got them.

The manual also has a note on Command-A, which ends the current game. It suggests using it on someone who is about to beat your high score.

faq.q: Is this the original Crystal Quest?
faq.a: It is version 2.2.5, the Macintosh release by Casady & Greene. Not the 2007 Xbox Live Arcade remake, which is a different program by different people.
With the mouse alone. The ship goes exactly where you point, and the button fires in whatever direction you are moving.

faq.q: Does it use the keyboard at all?
faq.a: For everything except flying. The mouse moves the ship, because absolute positioning is the point of the game. But the mouse button or any letter key fires, the space bar sets off a smart bomb, Tab pauses, and Command-S saves a game in progress.

Clear waves fast for the time bonus, catch the bonus crystals rather than shooting them, and save smart bombs for the waves that go wrong. Extra lives come every 15,000 points early on, then less often, so survival matters more the further you get.
Yes. The sampled voices are the first thing most people remember about it, and the sound files are still sitting on the disk with their 1994 copyright notices in the filenames.

intro:
A blank page, a ruler with tab stops you drag, and text that appears on screen in the typeface and size it will print in. That sounds like nothing. In 1984 it was the argument.

Every other word processor showed you a monospaced screen full of markup and asked you to imagine the result. MacWrite showed you the result. The phrase "what you see is what you get" stopped being a research demo and became something you could buy.

It is small. There is no spell check, no styles, no tables, no footnotes, and early versions capped a document at around eight pages because the whole thing had to fit in memory alongside the system.

What it has is the part that mattered: proportional type on screen, multiple fonts in one document, a ruler you manipulate directly, and a printed page that matches what you were looking at.

The ruler. Margins, indents and tab stops as objects you drag, rather than commands you type. Every word processor since has this and none of them invented it.

Cut, copy and paste on Cmd-X, C and V. Those three keys are next to each other at the bottom left of the keyboard for the same reason they always have been: so your left hand can reach them while your right hand stays on the mouse.

Mixed type in one document. Ordinary now. In 1984, on a machine most people were comparing to a typewriter, being able to put a heading in one face and the body in another was the demo that sold the computer.

Select by dragging, and by double-clicking a word. Also from here.

sections.h: Why a free word processor mattered
sections.html:
MacWrite and MacPaint shipped free with every Macintosh, which was a deliberate and expensive decision. The machine was new, it had almost no software, and nobody had used anything like it. Two good programs in the box meant that the first thing a buyer did was something the machine was unusually good at.

It also set a trap Apple later had to climb out of. Giving away a competent word processor made it hard for anyone else to sell one, until Microsoft Word arrived with the features MacWrite deliberately lacked and took the market permanently. Apple spun MacWrite out to Claris, which shipped MacWrite II and MacWrite Pro before discontinuing the line in the 1990s.

What survives is the interface. Open any word processor today and the ruler is still along the top, the fonts are still on a menu, and the page still shows you what you are going to get.

faq.a: Yes — Apple's release, the one that shipped with the Macintosh, running as it did in 1984.

faq.q: Why is my document limited in length?
faq.a: Early MacWrite held the whole document in memory alongside the system, which on a 128K machine meant a practical limit of around eight pages. It is a property of the program, not the emulation.
There isn't one. No styles, tables or footnotes either. The point of MacWrite was that the screen matched the page, and almost everything else was left out to make that fit.

faq.q: Why do Cmd-X, C and V work?
faq.a: Because this is where they come from. They are clustered at the bottom left of the keyboard so your left hand can reach them without leaving the mouse.

faq.q: Can I get text out of it?
faq.a: Only by retyping or screenshotting — the emulated Mac's disk lives in your browser and nothing is shared with your real machine.

The sequel to the game that proved the Macintosh could do action, and it is bigger in every direction: more rooms, a map to get lost in, an actual objective beyond surviving, and a jetpack.

It is also harder, which in the context of Dark Castle is a substantial claim.

This is one of the handful of titles here that runs on its own System rather than on the System 7.5.3 disk the rest use. Copied onto System 7 it boots to a black screen and stays there — no error, no bomb, just black. Its own 1987 System runs it perfectly.

The game shipped on two disks, the program and half its data on one and the rest on the other. Both have been merged onto a single bootable volume here, and the disk's own boot blocks were kept and pointed at the game, which is how a self-booting disk of that era launched straight into a title with no Finder in the way.

sections.h: What is different from Dark Castle
sections.html:
There is a goal. Dark Castle was a set of rooms to survive. Beyond has you collecting five orbs scattered through the castle and using them to reach the Black Knight, which means navigating rather than simply enduring.

The jetpack. A limited-fuel flight pack that opens up vertical routes and is entirely capable of flying you into something that kills you.

A map screen, because the castle is now large enough to get lost in.

More to do with the mouse. There are shields, bombs and a fireball weapon, on top of the rocks.

The engine, the art style and the punishing physics are all carried straight over, so anyone who has played the original will be immediately at home and immediately dying.

Jonathan Gay wrote it and Mark Stephen Pierce drew it, the pair who made the original. Gay was barely out of his teens at this point and would go on to build FutureSplash Animator, which Macromedia bought and renamed Flash — so the person responsible for these bats and this jetpack is also responsible for a decade of the animated web.

Pierce's art does more here than in the first game because there is more of it: the castle has genuine geography, and the cross-hatched one-bit style holds up across a much larger set of rooms than it was originally asked to.

faq.q: Do I need to play Dark Castle first?
faq.a: No, but it helps. Beyond assumes you already know the movement and the throwing, and it is not gentle about teaching them again.

faq.q: Why does it boot with no desktop?
faq.a: It runs from its own 1987 disk rather than the System 7 disk most titles here use, because under System 7 it comes up to a black screen and stays there. The disk's boot blocks name the game as the startup program, so the machine comes up in it.
Yes — the program and part of its data on one, the rest on the other. Both have been merged onto a single volume here so nothing asks you to swap disks.
Collect five orbs from around the castle and use them to reach and defeat the Black Knight.
Limited fuel, and it opens vertical routes you cannot reach on foot. It will also happily fly you into a hazard, so it is not a way out of trouble.
It is. Turn the difficulty down in the Options menu — the game was built for people who would spend weeks on it.

Start it on a colour screen without its MegaDraw acceleration and Crystal Crazy itself puts up a dialog explaining that it will not manage anything like full speed and would be more fun in black and white. The structure is Crystal Quest's: clear the board, reach the gate, next wave, harder. What changes is what "clear the board" means from wave to wave.

sections.h: Casady & Greene at the end of the Mac's middle age
sections.html:
By 1993 Casady & Greene had been publishing Mac-only software for a decade — Crystal Quest, Conflict Catcher, Spell Catcher, and later the first version of SoundJam MP, which Apple bought and turned into iTunes.

Crystal Crazy is what that house looked like at its most confident: a sequel nobody strictly needed, made carefully, shipped with its own accelerated drawing engine, and carrying a dialog that politely tells you your machine is not good enough for the colour mode.

The company closed in 2003. Patrick Buckland, who wrote both games, went on to found Rockstar Leeds.

faq.q: How is it different from Crystal Quest?
faq.a: More enemies, more weapons, and waves with varying objectives — crystals, smashing objects, assembling jigsaws — instead of the single collect-and-escape goal.

faq.q: Is it better than the original?
faq.a: Opinions differ. It is bigger and more varied; the original is leaner and more severe, and plenty of people prefer that.

Most of this site runs black-and-white software from the 1980s on compact Macs. This is the other end: 1999, colour, 800×600, and a PowerPC underneath.

This is a considerably bigger thing to start than the rest of the catalogue. A black-and-white game from 1986 is a few hundred kilobytes; this is a 500 MB disk with an entire operating system on it, so the first boot takes rather longer than a title does.

It is a real install and you can break it. Drag things to the Trash, rearrange the System Folder, change the desktop pattern — it is your copy, it lives in your browser, and reloading with fresh site data gives you a clean one.

The Appearance control panel. Mac OS 8 introduced Platinum, the grey three-dimensional look that replaced the flat black-and-white Finder of the previous thirteen years. This is where it is configured, and it was a genuinely new idea at the time.

Spring-loaded folders. Drag a file onto a folder and hold still — the folder springs open so you can drop it deeper. It came in with this line and it is still in macOS today.

Sherlock, in the Apple menu. Mac OS 8.5 rebuilt Find File into something that searched file contents and, startlingly for 1998, the internet, through plug-ins for individual search engines.

The Extensions folder. Open System Folder → Extensions and look at the size of it. Every one of those loaded at startup, in alphabetical order, and any one of them could bring the machine down. This is what "extension conflict" meant, and it is why these machines had a folder called Extensions (Disabled).

Pop-up windows. Drag a window to the bottom of the screen and it becomes a tab. This one did not survive.

sections.h: Where Mac OS 8.6 sits in the story
sections.html:
Mac OS 8 shipped in July 1997, and the timing is the interesting part. Apple was close to failing. Copland, the ground-up modern operating system that was supposed to replace the classic Mac OS, had collapsed after years of work. Apple had just bought NeXT, Steve Jobs was back, and the operating system that would actually solve the problem — Mac OS X — was still four years away.

Mac OS 8 is what Apple shipped in the meantime: the salvageable parts of Copland bolted onto the existing system. A multithreaded Finder, the Platinum appearance, spring-loaded folders, a rewritten networking stack. It sold around 1.2 million copies in two weeks, which for a paid OS upgrade in 1997 was remarkable, and it bought Apple the time it needed.

What runs here is 8.6, from May 1999 — the end of that line rather than the beginning. By then 8.1 had brought HFS Plus, which fixed a genuine problem: on the old filesystem a one-gigabyte disk allocated space in sixteen-kilobyte blocks, so a one-byte file consumed sixteen kilobytes and a drive full of small files wasted most of itself. 8.5 had brought Sherlock and dropped 68k support entirely, making this the first PowerPC-only Mac OS. 8.6 refined the nanokernel underneath and improved power management.

Mac OS 9 followed later that year, and then nothing: Mac OS X was a different operating system wearing the family name. This is close to the last word of the system that began in 1984.

faq.q: Is this a real Mac OS?
faq.a: Yes — a complete Mac OS 8.6 install, booting on an emulated Power Macintosh 9500 with a PowerPC 604. Not a mock-up or a simulation of the interface.
Because 8.6 is what this preserved disk holds, and it is the better end of the line to show: HFS Plus, Sherlock, and a refined nanokernel, all of which arrived across 8.1 to 8.6.

faq.q: Why does it take so long to start?
faq.a: Because it is a 500 MB disk with an operating system on it rather than a single small application. The chunks it needs first are prefetched, but it is still a real boot.
Yes, freely. It is your own copy living in your browser. Clearing site data gives you a fresh one.

faq.q: Can I put my own software on it?
faq.a: Not directly from this page — but the file loader will open a disk image you bring, on an emulated Mac of its own.

faq.q: Why a Power Macintosh and not a Quadra?
faq.a: Mac OS 8.5 and later dropped 68k support entirely — they are PowerPC-only. SheepShaver emulates a PowerPC 604, which is what this release was built for.
No. The emulated Mac has no network connection, so Internet Explorer and Outlook Express are there to look at rather than to use.

Apple has not sold Mac OS 8.6 in over twenty years and it runs on no machine Apple makes. Classic Apple system software has been distributed openly by major archives for years. The reasoning is written out in full and the takedown promise is unconditional.

You wake in a dungeon. The princess is in a tower. The vizier Jaffar has given her an hour to marry him or die, and the clock is the real one — sixty minutes of wall time for the entire game, and it keeps running while you fall on spikes.

This is the Macintosh version, in colour, and it moves like nothing else from its era because the animation was traced frame by frame from film of a real person.

The controls take a few minutes because the prince has weight. He does not stop when you release the key — he skids, and he falls off ledges you thought you had cleared. Holding Shift makes him move carefully, and learning when to use it is most of the game.

The sixty-minute limit runs across the whole game, not per level, and it persists through deaths. Dying restarts the level but not the clock, which is why the game is really about learning routes rather than surviving them.

sections.h: Why the animation looks like that
sections.html:
Mechner filmed his younger brother David running, jumping and climbing in a car park, then traced the footage frame by frame — a technique borrowed from animation called rotoscoping, and almost unheard of in games in 1989.

The result is a character who moves with real momentum: he leans into a run, catches himself on a ledge with his feet swinging, and staggers when he lands badly. Every platform game since has been compared to it, and games as recent as the Ori and Celeste lineage are working in a tradition this started.

It also cost enormously in memory — each frame of that animation had to be stored — which is why the levels are so spare. The trade was deliberate: fewer things on screen, and the one thing that is there moves like a person.

sections.h: Getting further than the first ten minutes
sections.html:
Hold Shift near edges. Walking carefully stops you skidding off, and the majority of early deaths are skids.

Take a run-up for wide gaps. A standing jump clears very little. Back up, run, and press up as you reach the edge.

The guards are a rhythm, not a race. Parry, strike, step back. Attacking wildly loses every time.

Drink the small potions, avoid the ones that look wrong. Red restores health, blue is usually poison, and the tall ones raise your maximum.

The clock does not stop. Sixty minutes for the whole game. If you are exploring carefully you are losing, which is a genuinely unusual thing for a game of this age to demand.

faq.q: Is this the original Prince of Persia?
faq.a: It is the 1992 Macintosh port of it, in colour. The Apple II original from 1989 came first and looks rather different; this is the version Mac owners played.
Completely. It covers the whole game, it keeps running while you are dead, and it is the reason the game is about learning routes rather than exploring them.

faq.q: Why is it so hard to control?
faq.a: The prince has momentum, deliberately. Hold Shift to move carefully, and take a run-up before any jump that looks long.
It is a rhythm. Parry with back, strike with forward, and wait for the opening rather than pressing constantly.

faq.q: Why does the animation look so smooth?
faq.a: Because it was rotoscoped — Jordan Mechner filmed his brother running and jumping, then traced the footage frame by frame.

Each level gives you a fixed number of each skill, a time limit, and a percentage you have to save. The lemmings walk, turn at walls, fall, and die if the fall is too far. Everything else is you.

The difficulty tiers — Fun, Tricky, Taxing, Mayhem — are not a gentle curve. Fun teaches you the skills; Mayhem assumes you have internalised them and starts removing the ones you want.

sections.h: The eight jobs, and what they are really for
sections.html:
Blocker stops everyone walking past, which is how you buy time. It also strands that lemming permanently unless you bomb him.

Builder lays a short staircase. Almost every level is really a question about where to put staircases.

Basher tunnels horizontally, miner diagonally down, digger straight down. Picking the wrong one of the three is the most common way to ruin a level.

Climber and floater are permanent upgrades to one lemming rather than actions — give them early to the one who will lead.

Bomber kills a lemming after five seconds and blows a hole in whatever he is standing on. It is both a demolition tool and the only way to undo a blocker.

Lemmings started as a throwaway experiment at DMA Design in Dundee: Mike Dailly drew a tiny sprite to see how small a recognisable walking character could be, and it turned out to be about eight pixels tall. Someone said you could make a game out of a lot of those, and Russell Kay said something to the effect that it would take about a year — which it did.

It sold in enormous numbers on the Amiga and was ported to nearly everything with a screen. DMA Design later became Rockstar North and made Grand Theft Auto, which is a fairly wide arc from small green creatures walking off cliffs.

The design idea that made it work is that you never control a lemming directly. You alter the environment and the rules, and the population does what populations do. It is closer to SimCity than to a platform game, dressed up as slapstick.

faq.a: It is the Macintosh port, in colour, with the full level set. The Amiga version came first and is the one usually shown in screenshots.

faq.q: How do I assign a skill?
faq.a: Click the skill in the bar at the bottom, then click the lemming you want to do it. The number above each skill is how many you have left.
Fun, Tricky, Taxing and Mayhem. Fun teaches the skills; Mayhem assumes you know them and takes away the ones you would rather use.

faq.q: How do I get rid of a blocker?
faq.a: Make him a bomber. It is the only way, it kills him, and the hole he leaves is often the point.
It blows up every lemming on the level. Click it twice to confirm. It is how you concede.

Mechanically identical to Lemmings — the same eight skills, the same rules, the same interface. What changes is the design of the levels, which assume you already know all of it.

Start here only if you have played the original. This was sold as an expansion to people who had finished a hundred and twenty levels, and it is built for them.

Five new tilesets — including a distinctly odd one built from what appear to be bones, and a bright cartoon set that makes the cruelty of the levels funnier.

Difficulty tiers renamed to Tame, Crazy, Wild, Wicked and Havoc. Tame corresponds roughly to the original's Tricky, so the whole thing is shifted up.

Level design that plays against your habits. The original taught you patterns; this one builds levels that look like those patterns and punish you for applying them.

There is no new mechanic, and that is the point — it is a hundred more puzzles written for an audience that had run out.

Selling a hundred extra levels as a separate product was not yet an established idea. Lemmings had sold in the millions, its audience had finished it, and DMA Design's answer was to make more of the same thing rather than a sequel with new systems.

It worked, and the pattern is now so normal that it is hard to see as a decision: the same engine, new content, sold to people who already own the original. The actual Lemmings sequels that followed — adding tribes, new skills, and elaborate settings — are much less well remembered than this expansion pack.

You drive a walking tank through angular, brightly coloured rooms, and the whole thing renders in flat-shaded polygons that look like nothing else from 1996. It was built for network play between Macs in an office or a lab, and it came with a level editor that people used hard.

Avara is one of the stranger things Ambrosia published, and one of the best.

sections.html:
MachinePower Macintosh 9500, 800×600 in colour
SystemMac OS 8.6, shared with every other title of this era
EmulatorSheepShaver, compiled to WebAssembly
Version1.0.1, as the Ambrosia installer produced it

This is the first title here that does not carry its own operating system. Mac OS 8.6 is mounted from one shared disk image, identical for every title of this era, and Avara sits on a small disk of its own beside it — so the operating system is downloaded once and the next Mac OS 8 title costs only its own few megabytes.

It is demanding. Avara renders its polygons in software on an emulated PowerPC, and the machine occasionally runs out of room and stops — if it does, reload the page and it starts again.

The shareware notice on startup is part of the software. Ambrosia's licence allows this to be distributed only unmodified, which means the notice stays exactly where it is. Click "Not Yet".

It is built around network play. Avara expected several Macs on the same network, each driving a hector — the bipedal machine you pilot — through a shared level. Single player works and ships with level sets, but the design points outward.

The rendering is flat-shaded polygons at a time when Mac action games were overwhelmingly sprites. No textures, strong colours, hard edges, and a readability that a lot of textured 3D from the same years lost.

The levels are a description language. Avara's levels are written rather than drawn, in a text format the game compiles, which is why the community produced so many of them. "Net Levels" and "Berserkir Fury" are both installed here.

Movement has weight. The hector walks, and turning, walking and aiming are separate things you do at once. It takes a few minutes and then it is the point.

Ambrosia Software was the great Macintosh shareware house: Maelstrom, Apeiron, Escape Velocity, SketchFighter, and a distribution model where you downloaded the whole game, played it, and paid if you kept it. Avara was written by Juri Munkki and published by Ambrosia in 1996.

In 2017 Munkki released Avara's source code, and a community port now runs it natively on modern machines with proper network play. What runs on this page is the original 1996 Macintosh application rather than that port — the thing as it shipped, nag screen and all.

Ambrosia itself wound down in 2017. Maelstrom, which is also on this site, is from the same house and under the same kind of licence.

A paddle, a ball, and a wall of bricks — and then everything else. Falling capsules that give you a wider paddle, a laser, a sticky bat or three balls at once. Bricks that need several hits. Evil bubbles that drift down and knock your ball off course.

MacBrickout is the Macintosh's definitive take on Breakout, and it is far more generous than it needs to be: a hundred-odd levels across three packs, all included here.

Like the other Mac OS 8 titles here, MacBrickout does not carry its own operating system. Mac OS 8.6 is mounted from one shared image identical for every title of this era, and MacBrickout sits on a small disk of its own beside it.

It is mouse-only and it wants a real mouse or trackpad — the paddle follows your hand directly, so a touchscreen is not much use.

Breakout on its own is a 1976 idea. What made the genre survive is Arkanoid's contribution in 1986: bricks that drop power-ups, so the board is constantly changing what you are able to do.

MacBrickout takes that seriously. There are capsules for a wider paddle, a laser, a slower ball, a catch-and-aim sticky bat, extra lives, and multiball. There are also capsules you do not want, which look much like the ones you do, and deciding whether to move under a falling capsule while a ball is in play is most of the skill.

The evil bubbles are the other half. They drift down the screen, they are not destroyed by your ball, and they deflect it — so a clean shot set up three seconds ago arrives somewhere else entirely.

sections.h: Three packs, and a development log
sections.html:
The game ships with Standard Levels, Mania Levels and the 3.0 Levels from the previous version, all installed here. Mania is the one that assumes you have finished the others.

It also ships with something unusual: a plain-text development log, kept daily from 1996 to 1999, recording what its author did each day. It opens with an explanation that he had picked up the habit writing weekly progress reports while working on Sega Saturn and PlayStation games, and could not break it.

It is a genuinely interesting document — a complete record of one person building a shareware game in their own time, including the rewrites, the collision-detection problems and the long break in the middle. That kind of thing is almost never preserved, and it is on the disk here.

A hand-drawn platformer with a genuinely beautiful look, built by one of the last great Macintosh shareware houses. You are Ferazel, an elf with a wand, digging through soil, climbing vines and casting spells across a world that is considerably larger than it first appears.

This is the demo version, which is what Ambrosia distributed freely and is licensed for use without a time limit.

Ferazel's Wand does not carry its own operating system. Mac OS 8.6 is mounted from one shared image identical for every title of this era, and the game sits on a small disk beside it — so the system is downloaded once and shared with Avara and MacBrickout.

The first thing it does is ask whether to switch to 640×480. The game was drawn for that size and looks right there; saying no leaves it in a window on the larger desktop.

This is the demo: the opening section of the game rather than the whole thing. Ambrosia licensed it for free use without a time limit, which is why it is the build here.

Digging. Most platformers give you solid ground and ask you to go over it. Ferazel digs through it, so the levels are a solid mass you tunnel into rather than a set of ledges, and the route is something you make.

The art. Every sprite and background is hand-drawn, and the palette is warm and specific in a way very little else from 1999 is. It is the reason people still bring the game up.

Spells. You collect and hold one at a time — fire, ice, a shield — and choosing which to carry into a room is a real decision rather than an inventory chore.

It is not short of secrets. The digging means whole areas can be hidden behind an ordinary-looking wall, and the demo already has several.

Ferazel's Wand came out in 1999, near the end of the Macintosh shareware era that Ambrosia Software had defined: Maelstrom in 1992, Apeiron, Escape Velocity, Avara, and a business built on letting you download the whole game and pay if you kept it.

It was written by Ben Spees, who drew it as well, and it is the kind of thing that only really happens when one person has control of every part. Ambrosia kept selling it into the Mac OS X years before winding down in 2017.

Two other Ambrosia titles are on this site: Maelstrom from 1992 and Avara from 1996. Between them they cover most of what that house was.

It is the most ambitious thing Ambrosia ever published, and one of the few Macintosh RPGs anyone still argues about.

Cythera does not carry its own operating system — Mac OS 8.6 comes from the shared image used by Avara, Ferazel's Wand and MacBrickout, so if you have opened one of those it starts much faster.

The thing to know going in: conversation is typed. People say things, and you ask them about words in what they said. There is no dialogue menu. It is closer to a text adventure bolted onto an RPG, and it is where most of the game's information lives.

The island is simulated, not staged. Characters keep schedules, shops open and close, and things happen whether or not you are there to see them. It is doing, in 1998 on a Macintosh, roughly what Ultima VII was praised for.

It does not explain itself. There is no quest log pushing you forward, and the main thread can be missed entirely for hours while you do something else. Opinions divide sharply on whether that is the point or the flaw.

Magic is a language. Spells are assembled from components you learn, rather than picked from a list, which means finding out what is possible is itself progress.

It was unfinished. Cythera shipped with its story only partly told and a sequel that never came. Knowing that in advance makes it a better experience rather than a worse one.

Ambrosia Software built its name on arcade games — Maelstrom, Apeiron, Swoop — and on Escape Velocity, which was a space trading game with a strong spine. Cythera is neither: a slow, text-heavy, deliberately obscure RPG by Glenn Andreas, published in 1998 into a Macintosh games market that was already thin.

It did not sell like Escape Velocity and it has a much smaller following, but the people who played it tend to remember it in detail. Three other Ambrosia titles are here: Maelstrom, Avara and Ferazel's Wand.

sections.h: The thing that makes it tense
sections.html:
A line under construction is vulnerable along its whole length. You are not dodging — you are committing to a route and then hoping nothing reaches it before you close the loop.

So the game is a constant argument with yourself about greed. A short line is safe and claims almost nothing. A long one across open board is worth the level and is exactly what gets you killed. Good players spend most of the level nibbling and then take one enormous risk when the bouncing things happen to be on the far side.

The percentage needed to clear rises, and the number of hazards rises with it, so the safe strategy stops being sufficient fairly quickly.

Barrack does what Ambrosia did to almost everything: take an arcade idea that already worked, rebuild it properly for the Macintosh, and spend an unreasonable amount of effort on how it looks and sounds. Maelstrom did it to Asteroids, Apeiron to Centipede, and Barrack to Qix.

The result is a game nobody needed that is markedly better made than the thing it copies. The riveted-metal presentation, the sound design and the high-score table are all doing more work than the genre requires.

Four other Ambrosia titles are on this site: Maelstrom, Avara, Cythera and Ferazel's Wand.

description: Archon, the 1984 Macintosh release of Free Fall's chess-and-combat hybrid, running in your browser on an emulated Macintosh Plus.

ogDescription: The 1984 Macintosh Archon, on an emulated Mac Plus.
h1: Archon — the board is only half the game
author: Free Fall Associates / Electronic Arts
intro:
Archon looks like chess and is not. You move pieces on an eight-by-eight board, but when two of them meet, the board disappears and the pieces fight it out in real time on an arena screen — a knight against a goblin, a dragon against a unicorn, each with its own speed, reach and weapon. Winning a square is a matter of aim as much as position.

The other half of the idea is the board itself. The light squares darken and the dark squares lighten on a cycle, and a piece fighting on its own colour is stronger. A duel you would lose on Tuesday you win on Thursday. Good players plan around the cycle; everyone else finds out about it the hard way.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
MachineMacintosh Plus, 512×342, black and white
SystemThe floppy's own — this disk carries the System it shipped with
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly
SavesNone. Archon is one sitting, as it was in 1984.

This is the black-and-white Macintosh Archon, not the colour Atari or Commodore version most people picture. The pieces are drawn in outline and the arena is white; it reads more like a woodcut than the arcade original, and the animation is slower.

It is also the reason this title boots the way it does. Archon predates almost everything System 7 expects an application to do, and copying it onto a modern-ish system disk makes the Macintosh reset on launch. Its own 1984 System is the only one it runs under, so the disk is served as it is.

It refused to be one genre. In 1983 a game was a strategy game or an action game, and Archon made you good at both or beat you. The design has been copied since — Archon Ultra, Unholy War, a dozen others — and none of them displaced it.

The pieces are not equal, on purpose. Chess balances by symmetry; Archon does not even try. Light gets knights and golems, Dark gets goblins and trolls, and the two sides play differently. Balance comes from the luminosity cycle and the spells, not from giving both players the same army.

Free Fall's names are worth knowing. Paul Reiche III went on to Star Control; Anne Westfall programmed it; Jon Freeman designed it. It was the first game Electronic Arts published, in the original album-sleeve packaging, and it is the one that made the case that EA's whole premise was right.

Take the Light side first — it moves first, and its pieces are easier to fly. Move onto squares of your own colour when you expect a fight, and try to keep your weakest pieces off dark squares while the cycle is against you.

The five power points, one at each corner and one in the middle, are the win condition: occupy all five and the game is yours, whatever is left on the board. A piece standing on one cannot be displaced by an ordinary attack, which makes them worth more than the material it costs to take them.

The spells are once each, per side, for the whole game. Teleport and Heal are the two beginners under-use; Imprison and Revive are the two they waste early and want back at the end.

title: Play Balance of Power Online — Crawford's Cold War Game
description: Chris Crawford's Balance of Power, the 1985 geopolitical simulation, running in your browser on an emulated Macintosh Plus.

ogDescription: Chris Crawford's Cold War simulation, on an emulated Mac Plus.
h1: Balance of Power — you do not win, you avoid losing
author: Chris Crawford / Mindscape
intro:
You are the United States or the Soviet Union, from 1986 to 1994, and your job is to accumulate prestige without starting a nuclear war. You send aid, you back insurgencies, you apply diplomatic pressure, and every one of those moves can be challenged by the other side. Back down and you lose prestige. Do not back down and the crisis escalates a step.

The famous part is what happens if you push one too far. The game ends, and it refuses to dramatise it: no mushroom cloud, no animation, just a line of text telling you that you have lost and that there is no scoring in a nuclear war. Crawford put it there deliberately and it is the single most quoted screen in 1980s computer gaming.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
MachineMacintosh Plus, 512×342, black and white
SystemThe floppy's own — this disk carries the System it shipped with
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly
SavesInside the emulated Mac, in your browser

This is a game of menus and a world map, and it does not explain itself gently. Every country has records for its government, its insurgency, its finances and its relations with both superpowers, and reading those is most of the game.

The application is named "Balance of Power" on the original floppy. The boot blocks that name a disk's startup program hold fifteen characters, so on this copy the file is called "Balance of Powe" — nothing else was altered, and you never see a Finder in which the shortened name would appear.

It took a position. Crawford was not making a wargame with a Cold War skin; he was arguing that the superpower relationship was a system with rules, and that the rules made brinkmanship a losing strategy. You can disagree with the thesis — plenty did — but the game is genuinely about something.

The losing screen. "You have just lost the game. However, there is no animated display of a mushroom cloud with parts of bodies flying through the air. We do not reward failure." It has been quoted, argued about and imitated for forty years.

It sold like a real game. Around a quarter of a million copies, with a companion book from Random House. A political simulation with no combat was, briefly, a mainstream hit.

Play the United States on the lowest difficulty first, and spend the first year doing nothing but reading. Open a few countries and look at what the game tracks about them; the interface is dense and the vocabulary is its own.

Prestige comes from having friendly governments in countries that matter. Small aid to a country nobody is contesting is cheap and safe; backing a coup in a country the other side cares about is where crises come from.

When the other side challenges you, the question is always the same: is this worth a step up the escalation ladder? Most of the time it is not. Learning to fold early, repeatedly, and still finish ahead on prestige is the whole skill of the game.

h1: Skyfox — fifteen scenarios and a very fast aeroplane
author: Ray Tobey / Dynamix / Electronic Arts
intro:
You fly the Skyfox, a fighter fast enough that the scenery arrives before you have decided what to do about it. Fifteen scenarios run from a single training flight up to a full invasion, and each one is a mix of dogfighting, ground attack and getting back to base before the base is gone.

Ray Tobey wrote the original when he was seventeen, and it was one of the games that made Electronic Arts' name. Dynamix did the Macintosh conversion, which is the version here: black and white, 512×342, and considerably starker than the colour originals.

This is the monochrome Macintosh conversion, not the Commodore 64 or Apple II version most screenshots online show. The horizon, the tanks and the enemy fighters are all line art, and the framerate is the framerate a 68000 could manage.

The disk carries its own 1985 System and boots straight into the game. Copying it onto a System 7 disk simply resets the machine, which is true of nearly everything from this period.

It was EA's showpiece for speed. In 1984 most home-computer flight games were slideshows. Skyfox moved, and the marketing leaned on it hard — the packaging is one of the best-known of EA's album-sleeve era.

Fifteen scenarios, not one sandbox. Each has its own set-up and its own way of going wrong, which gave it more life than the single endless mission most contemporaries offered.

Ray Tobey was seventeen. He wrote it on an Apple II, EA published it, and it sold well enough to be ported to nearly everything. That story was part of the appeal at the time and it is still a fair reason to look at the thing.

Start with the training scenario. The aircraft is fast enough that the first real mission will kill you before you have worked out which way you are pointing.

Learn the radar before you learn the guns. Skyfox is mostly a game about arriving in the right place — the shooting is straightforward once you are there, and the missions you lose are the ones where a tank column reached the base while you were somewhere else.

The automatic pilot will fly you to a contact. Use it constantly; it is not a cheat, it is how the game expects you to cover ground.

h1: Seven Cities of Gold — a whole continent, and no map
author: Ozark Softscape / Electronic Arts
intro:
You take a commission from the Spanish crown, fit out some ships, sail west and find out what is there. The coastline is drawn as you sail along it. The interior is blank until you walk into it. When you meet people, you can trade with them, ask them for guides, or attack them, and the game keeps score of all three without ever telling you which it approves of.

The map can be the real Americas or one the game invents, which in 1984 was an unusual thing for a program to offer and is still the feature people mention first. Playing the random map strips away everything you already know and leaves the actual game: you have limited food, a crew whose morale you can lose, and a king who expects gold.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
MachineMacintosh Plus, 512×342, black and white
SystemThe floppy's own — this disk carries the System it shipped with
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly

The opening menu offers a historical map, a random map, or world generation. The generator is the reason to come back: it builds a continent, populates it, and does not tell you what is on it.

The Macintosh version is black and white and slower than the eight-bit originals, and the interface is mouse-driven rather than joystick-driven, which suits it. Expeditions are a matter of clicking carefully rather than reacting.

Procedural generation, in 1984, as the selling point. Not a random dungeon — a continent, with coastlines, rivers, terrain and settlements, generated so that the exploration loop still worked. It is one of the earliest commercial games built around the idea.

It does not editorialise, and that is uncomfortable. Massacring a village is a button. It is often profitable and the game reports it without comment. Bunten said the intent was to let the player find out what they would do, and modern writing about the game spends most of its time on exactly that.

Dan Bunten's design reputation starts here. Later known as Danielle Bunten Berry and best remembered for M.U.L.E., Bunten made Seven Cities the commercial success that M.U.L.E. was not.

Take the historical map first so the geography is at least familiar, then switch to a generated world once you know the controls.

Chart the coast before you go inland. Coastline is cheap to map from a ship and it tells you where the rivers come out, which is where the settlements are.

Food and crew morale are the two things that end expeditions. Trade for food early and often, take guides when offered, and go home before you have to — a modest haul delivered is worth more than a large one that never reaches Spain.

description: The 1985 Macintosh Wizardry — Sir-Tech's ten-level dungeon and the party of six that goes into it — running in your browser.

h1: Wizardry — six characters go down, and often fewer come back
appName: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord
author: Sir-Tech Software
intro:
You make six characters, equip them out of almost no money, and walk them into a ten-level maze under the castle. The maze is drawn in wireframe from the front of the party, there is no automap, and if the whole party dies down there the bodies stay where they fell until another party goes and fetches them.

Wizardry is where the party-based dungeon crawl comes from. Everything with a marching order and a wireframe corridor — Bard's Tale, Might and Magic, Eye of the Beholder, most of the genre for a decade — is downstream of this.

Almost everything from 1985 on this site boots its own System. Wizardry will not: its original floppy produces a Sad Mac on an emulated Macintosh Plus, every time. The application runs perfectly well when copied onto a System 7.5.3 disk, which is what this is, so it comes up to a desktop for a moment first.

There is no automap. Graph paper is not a joke here — it is how the game was played, and the maze is designed on the assumption that you are drawing it.

It defined the form. A party of six, classes and alignments, a wireframe first-person maze, turn-based combat against ranked groups of monsters. Wizardry did all of it first on a personal computer and most of the genre simply adopted the template.

It is genuinely unkind. Characters die permanently, resurrection can fail and turn them to ash, and a total party kill leaves your equipment on the dungeon floor for whoever goes to get it. Nothing is softened.

It mattered enormously in Japan. Wizardry became a bigger franchise there than in its home market and directly shaped a generation of Japanese role-playing games, which is why remakes keep appearing.

Make a balanced party: two fighters at the front, a thief, a priest and a mage behind them, and a sixth of whatever you like. Roll until you get decent bonus points; there is no penalty for rerolling and the first few levels are brutal without it.

Buy armour before weapons. Surviving the first floor is a question of not being hit.

Go down one level, map a few corridors, come back and rest. Wizardry rewards short trips far more than deep ones, and the most common way to lose a party is being one fight further in than the spell points allowed.

title: Play Deadline Online — Infocom's Murder Mystery
description: Deadline, Infocom's 1982 murder mystery and the first of its detective games, running in your browser on an emulated Macintosh Plus.
keywords: deadline infocom, play deadline online, infocom mystery game, marc blank, text adventure mac
ogDescription: Infocom's murder mystery, on an emulated Mac Plus.
h1: Deadline — twelve hours to arrest someone
author: Infocom
intro:
Marshall Robner is dead in his locked study and you have until eight in the evening to arrest someone for it. Everyone in the house is somewhere at every moment, doing something, whether or not you are in the room — and that is the entire design. Deadline is a simulation with a clock, not a puzzle box.

You can follow a suspect. You can wait in a room to see who comes in. You can show one person an object you found in another person's wastebasket and watch them change their story. Every command costs a minute, which means investigating one thing is choosing not to investigate another.

The evidence folder is not here. Deadline shipped in a box with a coroner's report, interview transcripts, photographs and a torn scrap of paper, and those documents carry information the disk does not. They were the copy protection and they were also part of the game.

You can finish Deadline without them — people did it in 1982 by taking notes — but it is harder, and it is fair to know that going in. Scans of the folder are easy to find if you want the full thing.

It invented the genre for computers. Before Deadline, Infocom made fantasy and science fiction. This was the first mystery, the first game with a cast of characters who had their own schedules, and the first to be sold with a box of physical evidence — a format Infocom reused for years afterwards.

The characters run whether you watch or not. Mrs Robner makes a phone call at a particular time. Someone visits the house. Something is disposed of. Miss a moment and you miss it: there is no scripted scene waiting for you to arrive.

You can arrest the wrong person. The game lets you, and then tells you what actually happened. Most adventure games of the period would simply refuse; Deadline treats a wrong accusation as a real ending.

Search the study first, then the grounds under the study window. Ask Sergeant Duffy to analyse anything you find — that is what he is for, and the lab results take real in-game time to come back, so send things early.

Interrogate everyone about everyone. ASK MRS ROBNER ABOUT GEORGE is a different question from ASK GEORGE ABOUT MRS ROBNER, and the contradictions between the two are the case.

Save constantly, and save into different slots. Twelve hours pass quickly, and the most common way to lose is to reach eight o'clock with a strong suspicion and no evidence a court would accept.

author: Infocom
intro:
You are a postal clerk in a small seaside town called Festeron, delivering one last envelope at the end of a long shift. By the time you get where you are going, the town has been replaced by a considerably worse version of itself, and the cat is enormous.

Wishbringer was Infocom's answer to the complaint that its games were impossible. It is built so that a first-time player can finish it, and it does that without being thin — which is the hard part, and the reason it is still the game people are pointed at first.

Wishbringer shipped with a glow-in-the-dark plastic stone, a map of Festeron and a sealed envelope. The stone is the one people remember; it is not on the disk, and the game does not need it.

The Macintosh version's Commands menu is worth using. It lists the verbs the parser knows, which removes most of the guess-the-word frustration that puts people off the genre.

It can be finished twice, two different ways. The stone grants seven wishes, and every puzzle it solves can also be solved without it. Playing through on wishes is the gentle route; playing through having never used one is the real game, and the game notices.

Festeron turning into Witchville. The transformation is the best single idea in the game: the same map, the same people, everything slightly and horribly wrong. It is done in prose with no graphics at all and it works.

It was Brian Moriarty's first. He went on to Trinity, which is regarded as one of the finest things Infocom published, and later to Loom at Lucasfilm. Wishbringer is where the voice starts.

Deliver the envelope. That is the whole of your instructions and the game means it — the plot starts when you arrive.

Read room descriptions carefully and try the obvious thing first; Wishbringer is unusually fair, and if something looks like it should work it generally does.

Hold the wishes back. They are finite, the game is winnable without any of them, and the second playthrough — the one where you solve everything the hard way — is the reason this game has a reputation rather than just a recommendation.

h1: The Witness — twelve hours, one house, one storm
author: Infocom
intro:
February 1938, somewhere near Los Angeles, raining. You are a detective from the Homicide Department and you have been called to a house by a man who thinks someone is going to kill him. He is right, and it happens while you are there.

The Witness is the second of Infocom's mysteries, after Deadline, and it is the tighter one. Fewer rooms, fewer suspects, a shorter clock — and a much better-written opening. Stu Galley wrote the prose in flat Chandler cadence and it holds up considerably better than most attempts at that voice.

The Witness shipped with a National Detective Gazette, a matchbook, a telegram and a Physician's report. Those are not on the disk. Unlike Deadline, where the folder carried information you genuinely need, The Witness is close to self-contained — the feelies set the mood more than they carry clues.

Like all of Infocom's mysteries the clock runs on your commands. Standing still costs you nothing; typing does.

It is the best-written of the three mysteries. Deadline is the more ambitious simulation and Suspect has the better hook, but The Witness has the prose. The opening paragraphs — the rain, the search light, the Colt in your holster — are quoted more than anything else Infocom published outside Zork.

It is short on purpose. One house, one evening, a handful of people. After Deadline's sprawl, Infocom made a mystery you could actually hold in your head, and it is the one most often recommended to someone trying the genre for the first time.

The murder happens in front of you. You are not reconstructing a crime from the outside; you are present, and what you were doing at the time matters.

Explore the house before anything happens. You have a little time and you will want to know the layout when things speed up.

Pay attention to what people are wearing and what they are carrying, and write it down. The Witness rewards noticing detail more than it rewards exhaustive searching.

ASK and SHOW are the two verbs that move the case. ANALYZE hands a thing to Sergeant Duffy for the lab; the result takes in-game time, so send anything promising as soon as you have it rather than saving it up.

h1: Infidel — your workers have gone and the pyramid is still there
author: Infocom
intro:
You wake in a tent in the desert with a hangover and no crew. They have taken the supplies and walked out, because you are, as the game establishes in its first few paragraphs, a thoroughly unpleasant person to work for. The pyramid you came to loot is still out there, and you are going in alone.

Infidel is the first of Infocom's "Tales of Adventure" and the one that gets argued about. The puzzles are largely mechanical — hieroglyphs, a sundial, a great deal of careful mapping — and the ending is famous for refusing to reward you.

Infidel shipped with a fake archaeological package — a map, a letter, a beaded necklace. Those were physical and are not on the disk. The map in particular is useful; scans of it are easy to find and the game is meaningfully easier with one.

This is a game where you should be drawing your own map as you go. The pyramid's interior is regular and the puzzles depend on knowing which chamber is where.

The ending. Infidel finishes in a way that is still, forty years later, the standard example of a game refusing to give the player a victory. Saying more spoils it; it is the reason the game is discussed at all rather than merely remembered.

The protagonist is the villain. Infocom wrote a player character who is greedy, incompetent and disliked, and then made you spend the game as him. Almost nothing else in 1983 was willing to do that.

It is a pure puzzle box. No characters, no combat, no clock — just a structure and your understanding of it. If Deadline is Infocom's simulation, Infidel is its crossword.

Search the tent and the camp thoroughly before heading into the desert. What you leave behind you cannot go back for easily.

h1: Suspect — you did not do it and everyone thinks you did
author: Infocom
intro:
It is Halloween night at a Maryland horse farm, you are a journalist in a ridiculous cowboy costume, and within the hour you will be the prime suspect in a murder you did not commit. The police arrive on a timer and the only way out is to hand them someone else, with evidence.

Suspect is the third and best-structured of Infocom's mysteries. Deadline gave you a police badge and Duffy to run errands; here you have no authority at all, and everything you do looks worse the longer you are at large.

The guests move on their own schedules through a large house, whether or not you are watching. Following someone is a legitimate and often necessary tactic, and so is waiting in a room to see who arrives.

The clock is tight and the police do not negotiate. Expect to lose several times while you learn where everybody goes.

You are the suspect, not the detective. Inverting the role changes everything: you cannot demand answers, you cannot order a lab test, and being found somewhere you should not be actively harms you. It is a much better use of the mystery format than the two games before it.

The cast has its own evening. Everyone is going somewhere and doing something on a schedule. The mystery is assembled from what you happen to witness, and two playthroughs can look quite different.

Dave Lebling wrote it. Co-author of Zork, and the person who also wrote Suspended and Spellbreaker; Suspect is his tightest piece of construction.

ogDescription: Infocom's shipwreck treasure hunt, on an emulated Mac Plus.
h1: Cutthroats — everyone on this island wants the same wreck
author: Infocom
intro:
You are a diver on Hardscrabble Island, it is late, and a shipmate you have not seen for years knocks on your door with a book of shipwrecks and a proposition. From there it is a matter of equipment, money, tides and the fact that at least one person in the room intends to leave with everything.

Cutthroats gives you a real schedule to keep — a boat to hire, a dive to make at a particular time — and characters whose loyalty is a live question. It is one of Infocom's most underrated games and one of its hardest to finish cleanly.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect

SystemThe floppy's own — this disk carries the System it shipped with
EmulatorMini vMac, compiled to WebAssembly

The book of shipwrecks is not on the disk. Cutthroats shipped with "A History of the Hardscrabble Island Wrecks" and a tide table, and the game refers you to both for information it does not print on screen — depths, dates, what is supposed to be aboard.

It is playable without them but genuinely harder, more so than for most Infocom feelies. Scans are easy to find and worth having open.

The clock is a schedule, not a countdown. Things happen at particular times — the boat leaves, the tide turns, someone comes looking for you — and the game is about being in the right place rather than about hurrying.

h1: Pensate — every step you take, everything else moves too
author: John Besnard / Penguin Software
intro:
You have to get a piece from the bottom of a board to the top. Between you and the top are other pieces, each of which moves in a fixed way — like a knight, like a bishop, straight ahead — and every one of them takes a turn each time you take one. Touch any of them and you start the level again.

There is no randomness and no reaction time involved. Every position is solvable and every failure is yours. It is closer to a chess problem that moves than to an arcade game, and the title screen quotes Eden Phillpotts on the universe being full of magical things waiting for our wits to grow sharper, which is either charming or a warning.

The design survives. The "everything moves when you move" rule is the core of a whole modern genre of turn-based puzzle games, and Pensate is a clean, early, standalone statement of it.

crumb: Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego?
h1: Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego? — follow the clues, get the warrant
appName: Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego?
author: Brøderbund
intro:
A thief has taken something enormous — the Statue of Liberty's torch, the Crown Jewels, the Great Wall — and you have a week to follow them around the world and make an arrest. In each city you question three witnesses, who tell you what the suspect was wearing, what currency they asked about, what flag they were reading. From that you work out where they went next, and separately you build a description good enough to get a warrant.

The warrant is the part people forget. You can chase the right suspect to the right city and still lose, because you arrested someone you had no paperwork for. Deduction and evidence are two different jobs and the game grades both.
