The World Almanac is not here. The game shipped in a box with one, and it expects you to look up flags, currencies and landmarks in it. Without it you are relying on the clues plus your own geography — which is harder, and is how most people play it now.

This is the black-and-white Macintosh build, not the colour DOS version or the later CD-ROM remakes with video. It is the original design: text clues, a map, and a clock.

It taught geography by accident. Nobody set out to learn where Kathmandu is; they learned it because a witness mentioned a currency and the clock was running. It is the standard example of a game that educates without announcing that it is doing so, and it sold millions on that strength.

The warrant mechanic is the clever bit. Splitting "where is the suspect" from "can you prove who it is" gives the game two failure modes and makes the witness details matter twice.

It became everything else. A PBS game show, a cartoon, a Netflix series in 2019, and a sequence of sequels across every platform — all downstream of this. The original is still the one people mean.

Every case runs the same four steps, and knowing them turns the game from guesswork into police work.

1. The crime scene. You start in the city where something was stolen. Three places will talk to you — a bank, an embassy, a library, a harbour, whatever that city has. Each gives you one sentence. Some of those sentences are about where the suspect went; others are about who the suspect is. Learning to tell the two apart is the whole skill.

2. Destination clues. "She was asking about the rand." "He wanted to know about the Knesset." "She changed money into drachmas." These name a country by its currency, its parliament, its flag or its landmark. Three or four cities are offered under Connections; one of them fits the clue.

3. Suspect clues. "He had red hair." "She drives a limousine." "His hobby was tennis." These never help you travel. They go in the warrant, and they are the half people forget until they have cornered someone they cannot arrest.

4. The warrant. Open Police Dossiers, enter every suspect detail you have collected, and issue the warrant before you catch up. A warrant naming the wrong person is worse than none: you arrest an innocent party and the case is over.

The clock is the pressure. You have a week, travel burns hours, and questioning a witness costs time too. Flying to a city the clues did not point at is how most cases are lost — not by failing to identify the thief, but by running out of Friday.

Start a case from the Game menu and go to the crime scene first. The three witnesses there give you your only lead.

Write down every detail of the suspect — not just the destination clues. Hair colour, hobby, vehicle, the feature they are remembered by. You need those for the warrant and the game will not collect them for you.

Issue the warrant before you corner the suspect. Arriving in the right city without one is the classic way to lose a case you had already solved.

Watch the clock. Flying to the wrong city costs hours you do not get back, and a week goes quickly.

h1: Zap'T'Balls II — Pang, over a lake
author: Richard F. Bannister
intro:
A large red ball bounces across a photograph of a lake. You are a small man at the bottom of the screen with a harpoon. Hit the ball and it splits in two smaller ones; hit those and they split again; keep going until nothing is left, and do not let any of them land on you. That is Pang — Super Buster Bros. in the United States — and Zap'T'Balls II is Richard Bannister's Macintosh version of it.

By his own account he wrote it because he could not afford a copy of the Amstrad CPC game of the same name, and used it to learn C. He came back to it in 2002 to fix a scoring bug one registered user would not stop reporting, and this is that last version.

The game opens on a title card of gulls over water and waits. Start from the menu bar: File → New Game → Normal Mode. Help! Mode, on the same submenu, is the gentler option.

The status bar along the bottom keeps score, level, lives and a countdown timer — the timer is the part that catches people.

sections.h: Why it is worth a look
sections.html:
Photographs for backgrounds. Where most arcade games of 1994 drew their scenery, Zap'T'Balls uses real photographs, which gives it an odd, calm look for a game about being flattened by rubber balls.

The Sprite Animation Toolkit. It is built on Ingemar Ragnemalm's SAT, the free library behind a good part of Macintosh shareware action games in the 1990s. Richard Bannister credits it in the readme, and Space Debris, also here, uses it too.

An honest readme. Bannister describes his own graphics as terrible (of a sister game) and his old code as awful, and cut the shareware fee while he was at it. It is worth opening from the title disk.

File → New Game → Normal Mode.

Move with the arrow keys and fire straight up. Aim for the largest ball first while there is room to work, and do not stand directly under anything.

Watch the timer; running out costs a life as surely as a ball does.

It is an independently written Macintosh game in the same style as Pang, also known as Super Buster Bros. It borrows the idea, not the code or art.

h1: Sphaera — Breakout, over a pool of fire
author: Shawn Henry
intro:
A paddle at the bottom, a wall of bricks at the top, and a ball between them. Sphaera is Breakout, and says so in its readme — "a modern freeware arcade game in the spirit of the classic" — with the late-1990s additions you would expect: bricks that take several hits, gold ones that never break, bonuses that fall when a brick goes, and a pool of fire where the floor should be.

Shawn Henry released it as freeware in August 1999 and put out a bug-fix version a week later. That 1.0.1 release is the one here.

It opens on its title screen with a high-score table. Choose Game → New Game from the menu bar, then click or press Space to launch the ball.

The paddle follows the mouse or the arrow keys, depending on the setting in Options.

sections.h: What the bricks and bonuses do
sections.html:
From the readme: red, blue and green bricks go in one hit; grey bricks take several; gold bricks cannot be destroyed at all, and are there to shape the level.

Bonuses fall from broken bricks. The useful ones make your paddle larger, split the ball into three, let the paddle move up and down, set off a chain of explosions, or make the ball explosive so it ploughs through. One makes the paddle smaller — do not catch that one.

The side panel keeps score, lives, level, a multiplier and a bonus that counts down while you play.

Game → New Game, then click to launch.

If play stutters, the readme's own advice applies: there is a menu option to turn off background event handling, added in 1.0.1 for exactly that.

Clear the grey bricks early while you have room; the gold ones are permanent, so play the angles around them.
